Inference for the Youden curve of a multiply imputed biomarker: a band, a set of near-optimal cutoffs, and a corrected index

The seven paper-test answers are in the drafting log.

Abstract

Studies that impute a missing biomarker report the threshold where the averaged Youden curve peaks, without uncertainty, overstating its accuracy. We propose a band for the pooled curve by bootstrap-then-impute, a set of thresholds no other threshold beats beyond their difference’s uncertainty, and a bootstrap correction of the index. In simulation, the band covered the curve in 0.88 to 0.97 (MCSE at most 0.032) of replicates with normal imputation, but in 0.57 to 0.93 (MCSE at most 0.050) with predictive mean matching at 60% missing, where imputations were biased. The set held the best threshold in 0.93 to 1.00 (MCSE at most 0.026) at 0.33 to 0.85 of a band-based set’s length. Without missing data the index exceeded the chosen threshold’s accuracy by 0.013 to 0.043 (MCSE at most 0.005); the correction left 0.001 to 0.013 (MCSE at most 0.006). In NHANES, the cotinine set, 3.43 to 11.95 ng/mL, held the published 3.63 ng/mL cutoff.

Keywords: multiple imputation; Youden index; optimal cutoff; simultaneous confidence band; multiple comparisons with the best; bootstrap

1 Introduction

A threshold on a biomarker decides who is counted as having a condition: a threshold on serum cotinine, a metabolite of nicotine, separates people who smoke cigarettes from people who do not, and its value has been estimated from national survey data1,2. One criterion for the best threshold maximizes the sum of sensitivity and specificity, and that sum minus one is the Youden index3. When the biomarker is missing for some participants, multiple imputation, one of the most popular approaches to missing data4, fills in the missing values several times and analyses each completed dataset. In the paper that proposed nonparametric multiple imputation for ROC analysis, depression screening scores missing for part of a cohort of pregnant women were multiply imputed, the true and false positive rates were averaged across the completed datasets at each threshold, and one score was reported as “the unanimous optimum threshold”, with no statement of its uncertainty5. Applied studies impute a marker and then report an optimal cutoff6–8, and the two whose full text was read do not say how the completed datasets were combined6,7; many studies do not report the precision of their cutpoints at all9.

The reported index overstates the accuracy of the threshold it picks, because the threshold is chosen where the estimated curve happens to be high. With \(F_0\) and \(F_1\) the distribution functions of the marker among people without and with the condition, and a person called positive when the marker exceeds \(c\), the Youden curve, its best threshold, and its maximum are \[ \begin{aligned} J(c) &= F_0(c) - F_1(c), \\ c^* &= \arg\max_c J(c), \\ J^* &= J(c^*). \end{aligned} \] From \(L\) completed datasets the analyst averages the empirical curves \(\hat J_1, \dots, \hat J_L\) into \(\bar J\), takes the threshold \(\hat c\) at which \(\bar J\) peaks, and reports the peak, \(\max_c \bar J(c)\). Because \(\max_c \bar J(c) \ge \bar J(c^*)\) in every dataset and \(J(\hat c) \le J^*\), the reported index exceeds the true accuracy of the chosen threshold on average whenever the averaged curve is unbiased at \(c^*\): \[ \mathrm{E}\{\max_c \bar J(c)\} - \mathrm{E}\{J(\hat c)\} \;\ge\; \mathrm{E}\{\bar J(c^*)\} - J^* \;=\; 0 . \] Without missing data the empirical index has the largest upward bias of the usual estimators10, intervals exist for the index and the threshold11, and confidence regions exist for the sensitivity and specificity at the estimated threshold12. The empirical threshold converges at the cube-root rate to a non-normal limit CITE: the cube-root rate and the non-normal limit of an argmax of a step criterion (Kim and Pollard 1990; no readable text in Zotero)13, as does a weighted Youden threshold14. Rubin’s rules assume approximately normal estimates15, so they do not apply to the threshold, and the standard bootstrap is inconsistent for it13. When the disease status rather than the marker is missing, the ROC curve16 and intervals for the Youden index17,18 have been derived. When the marker is missing, imputation methods give the ROC curve and its area5,19,20. No method gives a band for the Youden curve, a set of thresholds that the data cannot separate from the best one, or a correction of the reported index from multiply imputed data.

This paper proposes all three and asks whether each works. The band estimates the covariance of the averaged curve by bootstrapping the data and imputing each resample4, and takes a sup-t critical value21. The near-optimal set keeps every threshold that no other threshold beats by more than the uncertainty of their difference, in the manner of multiple comparisons with the best22 CITE: multiple comparisons with the best (Hsu 1984; no PDF in Zotero). The correction subtracts a bootstrap estimate of the optimism CITE: the bootstrap estimate of optimism (Efron 1983; Harrell, Lee, and Mark 1996; no readable text in Zotero), with each resample imputed as many times as the analysis. A simulation study then asks four questions. Does the band cover the whole curve at the nominal rate, under predictive mean matching as well as under a correctly specified imputation model? Does the set contain the best threshold at least as often as its level promises, and how much narrower is it than the set the band itself gives? Does the correction remove the optimism of the reported index? And, as a note on the order of operations, how far apart are the index from averaging the curves first and the index from maximizing in each completed dataset first? An application to serum cotinine and smoking in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey CITE: the NHANES 2013 to 2018 data files (no item in Zotero) then asks whether the data can choose between a published cutoff and the cohort’s own.

2 Methods

2.1 The estimand

The question a threshold answers is how accurate it is, and the question a study answers is which threshold is most accurate. We therefore take as estimand the whole Youden curve and its peak, not one threshold. With \(F_d\) the distribution function of the marker \(X\) in group \(D = d\), and a person called positive when \(X > c\), the curve, its best threshold, and its maximum are \[ \begin{aligned} J(c) &= F_0(c) - F_1(c), \\ c^* &= \arg\max_c J(c), \\ J^* &= J(c^*). \end{aligned} \] A study that picks a threshold \(\hat c\) from data delivers the accuracy \(J(\hat c)\), which falls short of \(J^*\) by the regret \(J^* - J(\hat c)\). The marker is missing for some participants, at random given the disease status and observed covariates, and the disease status is always observed.

2.2 The pooled curve and its index

The analysis completes the data \(L\) times and averages the empirical curves of the completed datasets. With \(X_i^{(l)}\) the marker of participant \(i\) in completed dataset \(l\), observed or imputed, and \(n_d\) the size of group \(d\), \[ \begin{aligned} \hat F_{dl}(c) &= n_d^{-1} \textstyle\sum_{i : D_i = d} 1\{X_i^{(l)} \le c\}, \\ \hat J_l(c) &= \hat F_{0l}(c) - \hat F_{1l}(c), \\ \bar J(c) &= L^{-1} \textstyle\sum_{l=1}^{L} \hat J_l(c). \end{aligned} \] The pooled curve \(\bar J\) is a step function. The reported index is its maximum, \(\max_c \bar J(c)\), and the chosen threshold \(\hat c\) is the midpoint of the interval on which the maximum is reached, or the mean of those midpoints when several intervals tie. This is the procedure of Long, Zhang, and Hsu5, who averaged the curves of the completed datasets. The alternative, maximizing in each completed dataset first, reports the mean of the per-dataset maxima and the mean \(\tilde c = L^{-1} \sum_l \hat c_l\) of the per-dataset cutoffs.

At a fixed threshold the pooled curve is an average of differences of two proportions, so it is a regular estimate, and Rubin’s rules apply to it under proper imputation15. Its maximum is not regular. The reported index exceeds the accuracy the chosen threshold delivers, in expectation, whenever the pooled curve is unbiased at \(c^*\); the argument takes two lines (Supplementary note, S1.1). For the empirical curve the excess is of order \(n^{-2/3}\), because the empirical threshold converges at the cube-root rate CITE: the cube-root rate of an argmax of a step criterion (Kim and Pollard 1990; no readable text in Zotero)13 (S1.2). Maximizing first adds to that excess a gap that is never negative and is close to \(\kappa \hat B_c / 2\), with \(\kappa = -J''(c^*)\) the curvature at the peak and \(\hat B_c\) the variance of the per-dataset cutoffs (S1.3).

2.3 A band for the curve

A band that contains the whole curve with probability 95% brackets the accuracy of every threshold at once. We estimate the covariance of the pooled curve on a grid by bootstrapping the data and imputing each resample, whose variance estimates hold when the imputation and analysis models are uncongenial4, and we impute each resample only \(M\) times, which is enough when the variance is split into its parts23. The grid holds \(K = 41\) equally spaced thresholds \(c_1 < \dots < c_K\) between the 10% and 90% quantiles of all completed values. In each of \(R_B = 1,000\) resamples, drawn with replacement within each disease group, the resample is imputed \(M = 2\) times, giving curves \(\hat J_{b1}, \dots, \hat J_{bM}\) on the grid with mean \(\bar J_b\). Then \[ \begin{aligned} V &= \widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}_b(\bar J_b), \\ W &= R_B^{-1} \textstyle\sum_b (M - 1)^{-1} \sum_m (\hat J_{bm} - \bar J_b)(\hat J_{bm} - \bar J_b)^\top, \\ \Sigma &= V - W / M + W / L, \end{aligned} \] with negative eigenvalues of \(\Sigma\) set to zero. Here \(V\) is the covariance of an \(M\)-imputation estimate and \(W\) the covariance of one imputation about its resample’s mean, so \(\Sigma\) is the covariance of the \(L\)-imputation estimate the analysis reports (S1.4). With \(\mathrm{SE}_k = \Sigma_{kk}^{1/2}\), the band is \(\bar J(c_k) \pm q\,\mathrm{SE}_k\) for \(k = 1, \dots, K\), with a sup-t critical value \(q\)21. The bootstrap band takes \(q\) as the 95% quantile over resamples of \(\max_k \lvert \bar J_b(c_k) - m_k \rvert / V_{kk}^{1/2}\), with \(m\) the mean of the \(\bar J_b\). The hybrid band takes \(q\) as the same quantile of \(\max_k \lvert Z_k \rvert / \mathrm{SE}_k\) over 5,000 draws of \(Z \sim N(0, \Sigma)\).

We compared both with two bands built from Rubin’s rules24. The pointwise intervals combine, at each threshold, the binomial within-imputation variance of the two proportions with the between-imputation variance. The Rubin’s-rules band uses the whole covariance: the within-imputation covariance of an empirical distribution function, \(\{F(a) - F(a)F(b)\}/n\) for \(a \le b\), plus \((1 + 1/L)\) times the between-imputation covariance of the curves, with a sup-t critical value from the normal law. Because the within-imputation covariance of the empirical curve is known in closed form, this band also stands for imputing first and bootstrapping each completed dataset.

2.4 A set of near-optimal thresholds

The thresholds a study cannot tell apart from the best one are the useful answer to “which threshold”, and a band gives a first such set: the thresholds whose upper limit reaches the band’s highest lower limit, \(\{k : U_k \ge \max_j L_j\}\). That set uses the band’s width twice. The comparison-based set compares thresholds with each other, in the manner of multiple comparisons with the best22 CITE: multiple comparisons with the best (Hsu 1984; no PDF in Zotero). With \(\mathrm{SE}_{jk} = (\Sigma_{jj} + \Sigma_{kk} - 2 \Sigma_{jk})^{1/2}\) the standard error of the difference between thresholds \(j\) and \(k\), a threshold stays in the set unless another beats it by more than its critical value: \[ S_C = \{ k : \bar J(c_j) - \bar J(c_k) \le q_D\,\mathrm{SE}_{jk} \text{ for every } j \ne k \}. \] Nearby thresholds share most of their errors, so \(\mathrm{SE}_{jk}\) is small where \(c_j\) is close to \(c_k\), and \(S_C\) is narrower than the band-based set. For each grid point \(k\), let \(q_k\) be the 95% quantile of \(\max_{j \ne k} (D_j - D_k)/s_{jk}\), over the centred resample means with \(s_{jk}\) from \(V\) (bootstrap) or over draws of \(N(0, \Sigma)\) with \(s_{jk} = \mathrm{SE}_{jk}\) (hybrid). The critical value \(q_D = \max_k q_k\) guarantees that the grid’s best threshold is in the set whenever the comparisons involving it hold (S1.5); the plug-in value \(q_D = q_{\hat k}\), at the estimated best grid point \(\hat k\), is smaller.

2.5 A correction of the reported index

The bootstrap estimates how far a maximum overshoots by repeating the whole analysis on resamples and measuring each resample’s overshoot against the original data CITE: the bootstrap estimate of optimism (Efron 1983; Harrell, Lee, and Mark 1996; no readable text in Zotero). In each of \(R_O = 100\) further resamples, drawn within disease groups and imputed \(L\) times as the analysis is, we took the resample’s pooled curve \(\bar J_b\) and its maximizer \(\hat c_b\), and computed \[ \begin{aligned} o_b &= \bar J_b(\hat c_b) - \bar J(\hat c_b), \\ \hat J_{\mathrm{corr}} &= \bar J(\hat c) - R_O^{-1} \textstyle\sum_b o_b . \end{aligned} \] The correction starts from the pooled curve at the chosen threshold, which equals the maximum unless tied intervals lie apart. The same correction from the first \(200\) curve resamples, imputed \(M\) times each, was computed for comparison. The standard bootstrap does not reproduce the distribution of a cube-root estimator13, so whether the correction removes the optimism is a question for the simulation, not a property of the method.

2.6 The order of pooling

For the note on the order of operations, we also recorded the mean of the per-dataset cutoffs \(\tilde c\) and of the per-dataset maxima, the variance \(\hat B_c = L^{-1} \sum_l (\hat c_l - \tilde c)^2\), and a bagged cutoff, the mean of the cutoffs \(\hat c_b\) of the \(R_O\) correction resamples, the resampling analogue of maximizing first25.

2.7 Data

The application used the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) cycles 2013 to 2014, 2015 to 2016, and 2017 to 2018 CITE: the NHANES 2013 to 2018 data files (no item in Zotero): the serum cotinine laboratory files, the smoking questionnaire, and the demographics files, downloaded from the survey’s public data pages. The cohort was every participant aged eighteen or over who answered whether they had smoked one hundred cigarettes in their life; a current smoker had, and now smoked every day or some days, and everyone else who answered was a nonsmoker. The three cycles measured cotinine with the same laboratory method and limit of detection, and values below the limit are stored at the limit divided by the square root of two. The marker was log10 cotinine in ng/mL. The cohort held 17,948 adults, 3,353 of them current smokers, and cotinine was missing for 1,715 (9.6%).

Missing cotinine was imputed by predictive mean matching26 with five donors on smoking status, age and its square, sex, the interactions of smoking status with age and sex, race/ethnicity, cycle, education, and the ratio of family income to poverty, with refused, unknown, and unasked education and income as their own category. The analysis of the real missing values was repeated on the complete cases without imputation, as a benchmark, and on the complete cases with 40% of cotinine values set missing at random, with probability \(\mathrm{expit}(\alpha_0 + 0.5 D - 0.3 a + 0.2 m)\), \(a\) the standardized age and \(m\) the male indicator, so that the complete-case curve is the truth the analysis should recover. For each race/ethnicity group \(v\) the analysis was run within the group. Its stratum-specific cutoff maximizes \(\bar F_0(c \mid v) - \bar F_1(c \mid v)\). Its population-optimal cutoff maximizes \(w_0(v) \bar F_0(c \mid v) - w_1(v) \bar F_1(c \mid v)\), with \(w_d(v)\) the group’s share of all participants with \(D = d\); one such cutoff per group maximizes the Youden index of the whole population (S1.6). No survey weights were used: the estimand is the curve in the sample’s population, as in the simulation.

2.8 Software and reproducibility

The code is organized as a research compendium27: an R package whose functions are documented and tested, analysis scripts that call those functions and write every result to a results folder, and this manuscript, which reads only from that folder, so that every number, table, and figure in it is computed from the saved results when the document is rendered. Each simulation cell has its own random seed, derived from the design table, and the per-replicate results are saved rather than summaries. The software and package versions used are recorded with the results.

The analyses used R version 4.5.2 (2025-10-31) and the R package mice version 3.19.026 for both imputation engines. TO CONFIRM: the repository URL, withheld while review is double-anonymized

3 Simulation study

3.1 Design

The simulation study is reported in the ADEMP structure28: aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods, and performance measures, with a Monte Carlo standard error for every reported rate and average.

Aims. The study asked four questions, in the order of the Introduction. Does the bootstrap band, or the hybrid band, cover the whole curve in 95% of replicates, under predictive mean matching as under a correctly specified imputation model? Does the comparison-based set hold the grid’s best threshold at least that often, and how long is it? Does the matched correction remove the optimism of the reported index? And how large is the gap between the two orders of pooling, against \(\kappa \hat B_c / 2\)?

Data-generating mechanisms. The marker was normal in each group, \(X \mid D = 0 \sim N(0, 1)\) and \(X \mid D = 1 \sim N(\delta, \sigma_1^2)\), with an auxiliary variable \(Z = X + e\), \(e \sim N(0, 1)\), observed for everyone. The marker was missing with probability \(\mathrm{expit}(\alpha_0 + Z + 0.5 D)\), at random given \(Z\) and \(D\), and above all at high values of the marker, where donors for predictive mean matching are sparse; \(\alpha_0\) was solved for each target fraction. Table 1 lists the factors varied, their levels, and the reason for each. The design had five arms, 44 cells in all: the three shapes at 250 per group, each with a cell without missing values and the three missing fractions crossed with the two main imputation engines; the sharp shape at 100 and 1,000 per group with the same cells; the sharp shape with ten donors, and with complete cases, at the three missing fractions; and the sharp shape with 100 cases and 400 controls. Fixed were \(L = 20\) imputations, the empirical estimator, the auxiliary’s strength, and the missingness coefficients, as in an applied analysis with one strong auxiliary. In every cell without missing values the completed datasets are identical, so the bands are complete-data bands and the gap between the orders of pooling is exactly zero.

Estimands. The Youden curve \(J\) on each replicate’s grid, the grid’s best threshold \(c_{k^*}\) with \(k^* = \arg\max_k J(c_k)\), the maximum \(J^*\), and the accuracy \(J(\hat c)\) of the chosen threshold.

Methods. In every replicate, the procedure of the Methods with \(L = 20\), \(K = 41\), \(R_B = 1,000\) resamples with \(M = 2\) imputations each, and \(R_O = 100\) correction resamples: the pointwise intervals, the Rubin’s-rules band, the bootstrap band, and the hybrid band; the band-based set and the comparison-based set of each construction, the latter with the largest and with the plug-in critical value; the reported index, the matched correction, and the two-imputation correction; the pooled, averaged, and bagged cutoffs. Predictive mean matching used type 1 matching with five or ten donors, and normal imputation drew the regression parameters and then the missing values; both used \(D\), \(Z\), and \(D \times Z\) as predictors26. Complete cases ran the same procedure without imputation on the participants with the marker observed.

Performance measures. For each band, its simultaneous coverage, the share of replicates in which it contained the true curve at every grid point, and its mean half-width. For each set, the share of replicates in which it held \(c_{k^*}\), its mean length (the number of grid points times the grid step), and its length against the band-based set’s and against the length of the true range of thresholds within 0.01 of \(J^*\). For each index, its mean minus \(J(\hat c)\): the optimism of the reported index, and the bias of each corrected index. For each cutoff, its bias, empirical standard error, and root mean squared error against \(c^*\). For the pooling order, the mean gap against the mean of \(\kappa \hat B_c / 2\). At \(c_{k^*}\), the averaged curve’s bias, and the ratio of its Monte Carlo standard deviation to its mean standard error from \(\Sigma\) and from Rubin’s rules, which tells a biased curve from an underestimated variance. A difference was called nonzero only when it exceeded three Monte Carlo standard errors.

Replicates. The study used 100 replicates per cell, in seeded blocks so that results do not depend on the computer that ran them; the Monte Carlo standard error of a coverage near 0.95 is then 0.022. The protocol’s production design has 2,000 replicates per cell, a Monte Carlo standard error of 0.005.

3.2 Results

3.2.1 The bands

Without missing values the bands are complete-data bands, and the hybrid band covered the whole curve in 0.86 to 0.97 (MCSE at most 0.035) of replicates across shapes, sizes, and balance (Figure 1). The lowest, 0.86 (MCSE 0.035), was at 100 per group TO CONFIRM: whether the band undercovers at 100 per group without missing values; the shortfall from 0.95 is under three Monte Carlo standard errors at 100 replicates. With normal imputation the hybrid band covered in 0.88 to 0.97 (MCSE at most 0.032) of replicates and the bootstrap band in 0.90 to 0.97 (MCSE at most 0.030). With predictive mean matching the hybrid band covered in 0.90 to 0.97 (MCSE at most 0.030) of replicates at 20% and 40% missing, and in 0.57 to 0.93 (MCSE at most 0.050) at 60%, lowest for the flat shape. Ten donors in place of five gave 0.79 to 0.92 at the three missing fractions. The Rubin’s-rules band covered in 0.94 to 1.00 of replicates with normal imputation and in 0.01 to 0.95 with predictive mean matching, the pointwise intervals read as a band in at most 0.84, and the bands of the complete cases in 0.12 to 0.28.

Where the bands fell short under predictive mean matching, the averaged curve was biased at the best threshold, while its standard error matched its Monte Carlo spread (Table 2). At the grid’s best threshold the bias of the averaged curve reached -0.130 (MCSE 0.0111) in the flat shape at 60% missing (Table S1). Across every cell with imputed values, the Monte Carlo standard deviation of the averaged curve there was 0.84 to 1.11 times the mean standard error from the bootstrap-then-impute covariance. The same ratio for the Rubin’s-rules standard error reached 2.32 under predictive mean matching. Under the missingness model, 20% missing overall meant 6% of controls and 34% of cases for the sharp shape, and 60% overall meant 39% and 81%.

3.2.2 The near-optimal sets

The hybrid comparison-based set held the grid’s best threshold in 0.93 to 1.00 (MCSE at most 0.026) of replicates across all cells, and the bootstrap one in 0.93 to 1.00 (MCSE at most 0.026) (Figure 2). The hybrid set’s length was 0.33 to 0.85 of the band-based set’s, and 1.4 to 6.1 times the length of the true range of thresholds whose index is within 0.01 of \(J^*\). Without missing values in the sharp shape, its length fell from 1.41 at 100 per group to 0.66 at 1,000. The plug-in critical value, 2.55 to 2.75 across cells against 2.61 to 3.77 for the largest per-point quantile, shortened the hybrid set to 0.33 to 0.71 of the band-based set’s length, and that set held the best threshold in 0.91 to 1.00 (MCSE at most 0.029) of replicates.

3.2.3 The corrected index

Without missing values the reported index exceeded the true accuracy of the chosen threshold by 0.013 to 0.043 (MCSE at most 0.005) (Figure 3). For the sharp shape the optimism fell with group size, from 0.043 (MCSE 0.0050) at 100 per group to 0.013 (MCSE 0.0016) at 1,000, a slope of -0.52 (MCSE 0.073) on the log scale TO CONFIRM: the slope lies between minus one half and the minus two thirds of Supplementary note S1.2 within the precision of 100 replicates. The correction with 20 imputations per resample left 0.001 to 0.013 (MCSE at most 0.006) in those cells. With normal imputation the optimism was 0.002 to 0.039 (MCSE at most 0.006) and the corrected index’s bias -0.006 to 0.014 (MCSE at most 0.007). With predictive mean matching the corrected index’s bias was -0.053 to 0.015 (MCSE at most 0.010), lowest where the averaged curve was most biased. The correction with 2 imputations per resample had a bias of -0.057 to 0.013 (MCSE at most 0.011) across all cells.

3.2.4 The order of pooling

Maximizing in each completed dataset first raised the index above the pooled maximum by 0.0004 to 0.0161 (MCSE at most 0.001) in the cells with imputed values (Figure 4). The gap was 0.52 to 0.95 times the mean of \(\kappa \hat B_c / 2\) under predictive mean matching and 0.61 to 1.82 times under normal imputation. The averaged cutoff’s root mean squared error was 0.72 to 0.90 of the pooled cutoff’s, and the bagged cutoff’s 0.60 to 0.94 (Table S2).

4 Application

4.1 Data and comparison

The application asks the question of the Introduction on real data: which serum cotinine threshold separates people who smoke cigarettes from people who do not, and how sure can a study be of it, when cotinine is missing for some participants. The cohort, its definitions, and the imputation model are in the Methods. Of the 17,948 adults, 3,353 were current smokers, and cotinine was missing for 10.0% of smokers and 9.4% of nonsmokers. Table 3 places the data on the simulation’s gradients: the complete-case curve is as high as the separated shape’s and as flat at its peak as the flat shape’s, the groups are larger than the largest simulated size, and the real missing fraction, spread evenly over the two groups, is below the smallest simulated one, which falls on the cases above all.

4.2 The data cannot choose between the published cutoff and the cohort’s own

With the real missing values imputed, the pooled curve peaked at 7.37 ng/mL, where its index was 0.867 (Figure 5, left). The matched correction lowered the index by 0.0013, to 0.866. The comparison-based set of the hybrid construction ran from 3.43 to 11.95 ng/mL, and that of the bootstrap construction was the same; the band-based set ran from 0.77 to 25.27 ng/mL. The adult cutoff of 3.63 ng/mL published from the 2009 to 2014 cycles2 lay inside every set. A study that reports the cohort’s optimum as the cutoff therefore reports one point of a range that the data cannot narrow further, and the published cutoff, whose complete-case index is lower by 0.003, is as well supported.

With 39.8% of the complete cases’ cotinine values set missing at random, depending on smoking status, age, and sex only, a weaker dependence than the simulation’s, the analysis recovered the complete-case curve (Figure 5, right). The bootstrap band, the hybrid band, the Rubin’s-rules band, and even the pointwise intervals contained the complete-case curve at every grid point, and every set held the complete-case curve’s best grid threshold. The reported index, 0.874, exceeded the complete-case curve at the chosen threshold, 0.868, by 0.006, and the correction removed 0.0001 of it. In this analysis the hybrid comparison critical value rose to 5.15, against 2.75 for the plug-in value, and the hybrid comparison-based set widened to 1.00 to 25.76 ng/mL, while the bootstrap and plug-in sets ran from 1.64 to 15.61 ng/mL.

By race/ethnicity, the stratum-specific cutoffs ranged from 0.63 to 25.00 ng/mL (Table 4), and the published cutoff lay in the comparison-based set of 5 of the 6 groups. The population-optimal cutoff differed from the stratum-specific one in 4 groups, upward where the group held a larger share of the nonsmokers than of the smokers and downward where it held a smaller share, as S1.6 predicts.

5 Discussion

Table 5 sets what this paper adds beside what was known. The four questions of the Introduction have these answers, on 100 replicates per cell. Does the band cover the whole curve at the nominal rate, under predictive mean matching as well as under a correctly specified imputation model? Under the correct model, and without missing values, it covered close to the nominal rate; under predictive mean matching it did so at low missing fractions and fell short where the averaged curve itself was biased, at the highest missing fraction. Does the set contain the best threshold at least as often as its level promises, and how much narrower is it than the set the band itself gives? It held the best threshold at least as often as the level promises in every cell, at about half the length of the band-based set, yet still several times longer than the range of thresholds that are truly near-optimal. Does the correction remove the optimism of the reported index? It removed most of it without missing values and under the correct model, and overcorrected where the imputations were biased. How far apart are the index from averaging the curves first and the index from maximizing in each completed dataset first? By a few thousandths of the index, close to \(\kappa \hat B_c / 2\), while maximizing first, or bagging, gave a more accurate threshold.

For a study that imputes a missing marker and reports a cutoff, three changes follow. Report the pooled curve with its band and the comparison-based set, so that readers see the range of thresholds the data support, as in the cotinine example, where the published cutoff and the cohort’s own both fell in the set. Report the corrected index beside the maximum. And treat the imputation model as part of the inference: the bootstrap-then-impute covariance tracked the curve’s variance in every cell, so a band that undercovers points to imputations that are biased near the threshold, which ten donors, the pool recommended against sparse donors29, did not fix, and which a correctly specified model avoided TO CONFIRM: this reading rests on the normal engine being the correct model in the simulation; no misspecified parametric model was tried. Complete cases are not an alternative when missingness depends on the marker’s correlates: their bands missed the curve in most replicates.

Several features of the simulation limit what it shows. The marker was binormal, while real markers are skewed or, like cotinine below its limit of detection, carry a point mass; the application has one, the simulation does not. The auxiliary’s strength and the missingness coefficients were fixed, so the band’s shortfall under predictive mean matching was measured at one level of donor sparsity per missing fraction. The imputation model had one auxiliary and, for the normal engine, was correctly specified; real imputation models carry several covariates and are misspecified to some degree. Missingness was at random given the auxiliary and the disease status, and missingness that depends on the marker’s own value is corrected by neither engine. The covariance was always estimated from two imputations per resample and rescaled, and the number of resamples and of imputations per resample was not varied. The set’s guarantee is for the grid’s best threshold, not for \(c^*\) itself, and the grid had one resolution.

Several directions lie outside this paper. A second dataset is needed to test the procedure on a marker with another shape. A continuous covariate turns the stratum-specific cutoffs of the application into a covariate-specific curve35,36. When the disease status rather than the marker is missing, the same questions arise under verification bias16,17. Criteria other than the Youden index, such as a target sensitivity, need their own sets. A bootstrap with a theory for cube-root estimators13, carried through imputation, is the candidate for removing the optimism the plain correction leaves. A software release of the procedure, and a short reporting guide for applied studies that impute a marker and report a cutoff, are the steps that make the procedure usable.

Supplementary note S1

This note derives the six results the paper uses: why the reported index overstates the chosen threshold’s accuracy, how fast that excess shrinks, how far maximizing first moves the index, why the covariance split targets the analysis’s own estimate, why the comparison-based set holds the best threshold, and why one cutoff per stratum can be chosen stratum by stratum. Each is short, and each is checked by a test in the package or by the simulation.

Notation: \(J\), \(c^*\), \(J^*\), \(\bar J\), \(\hat c\), \(\hat J_l\), \(\hat c_l\), \(\Sigma\), \(V\), \(W\), \(M\), \(L\), and \(\mathrm{SE}_{jk}\) are as in the Methods, and \(n\) is the size of each group.

S1.1 The reported index is optimistic

If the pooled curve is unbiased at the best threshold, \(\mathrm{E}\{\bar J(c^*)\} = J^*\), then the reported index exceeds the accuracy of the chosen threshold in expectation: \[ \begin{aligned} \max_c \bar J(c) &\ge \bar J(c^*), \\ \mathrm{E}\{\max_c \bar J(c)\} &\ge \mathrm{E}\{\bar J(c^*)\} = J^*, \\ J^* &\ge J(\hat c), \\ \mathrm{E}\{\max_c \bar J(c)\} - \mathrm{E}\{J(\hat c)\} &\ge 0 . \end{aligned} \] Line 1 holds in every dataset, since a maximum is at least the value at any point. Line 2 takes expectations and uses the premise. Line 3 holds because \(J^*\) is the maximum of \(J\). Line 4 combines lines 2 and 3. The premise fails when the imputations are biased, which is the case the predictive-mean-matching cells probe. The paper uses the result in the Introduction and the Methods; the test that RunReplicateC() returns a maximum at least the curve’s value at the chosen threshold checks the first line in code, and the null cells of the simulation show the excess with nothing missing.

S1.2 The excess is of order \(n^{-2/3}\) (a sketch)

This is a sketch, not a proof. Assume complete data, a unique maximum with curvature \(\kappa = -J''(c^*) > 0\), and positive densities at \(c^*\). The empirical threshold maximizes a sum of indicator functions, the setting of cube-root asymptotics: \(n^{1/3}(\hat c - c^*)\) converges to the maximizer of a Gaussian process with a quadratic drift CITE: the cube-root limit (Kim and Pollard 1990; no readable text in Zotero)13. Write \(G = \bar J - J\) for the centred curve. Then \[ \begin{aligned} \max_c \bar J(c) - J(\hat c) &= \{\max_c \bar J(c) - \bar J(\hat c)\} + G(\hat c), \\ G(\hat c) &= G(c^*) + \{G(\hat c) - G(c^*)\}, \\ \mathrm{E}\{G(c^*)\} &= 0, \\ G(\hat c) - G(c^*) &= O_p(n^{-1/2} \lvert \hat c - c^* \rvert^{1/2}) = O_p(n^{-2/3}). \end{aligned} \] Line 1 adds and subtracts \(\bar J(\hat c)\); the braced term is zero when the maximum is reached at \(\hat c\), and of lower order when tied intervals lie apart. Line 2 adds and subtracts \(G(c^*)\). Line 3 holds because \(\bar J(c^*)\) is an average of unbiased proportions. Line 4 uses the modulus of continuity of the empirical process, whose increment over a distance \(\delta\) has standard deviation of order \((\delta / n)^{1/2}\), with \(\delta = O_p(n^{-1/3})\). The excess is therefore of order \(n^{-2/3}\) in expectation, given uniform integrability, which the sketch assumes. A full derivation must also carry the imputation: proper imputation with an unbiased model inflates the variance of \(G\) without changing its order. The paper uses the order in the Methods; the simulation’s size gradient checks it, since the optimism at the three sizes of the sharp shape should fall along a line of slope near \(-2/3\) on the log scale.

S1.3 The order of pooling

The mean of the per-dataset maxima is never below the maximum of the mean curve, and for curves that are quadratic near their peaks the gap is close to \(\kappa \hat B_c / 2\): \[ \begin{aligned} \hat J_l(c) &\le \max_{c'} \hat J_l(c') \quad \text{for every } c, l, \\ \bar J(c) &\le L^{-1} \textstyle\sum_l \max_{c'} \hat J_l(c') \quad \text{for every } c, \\ \max_c \bar J(c) &\le L^{-1} \textstyle\sum_l \max_{c'} \hat J_l(c'), \\ \hat J_l(c) &= m_l - (\kappa_l / 2)(c - \hat c_l)^2 \quad \text{near the peaks}, \\ \arg\max_c \bar J(c) &= \tilde c_\kappa = \textstyle\sum_l \kappa_l \hat c_l / \sum_l \kappa_l, \\ L^{-1} \textstyle\sum_l m_l - \max_c \bar J(c) &= L^{-1} \textstyle\sum_l (\kappa_l / 2)(\hat c_l - \tilde c_\kappa)^2 . \end{aligned} \] Line 1 is the definition of a maximum. Line 2 averages line 1 over \(l\). Line 3 maximizes the left side of line 2 over \(c\), so the gap is never negative; it is zero when one threshold maximizes every curve, as in the cells without missing values. Line 4 is the quadratic approximation, valid for smooth curves with every per-dataset cutoff in the region where it holds. Line 5 sets the derivative of the averaged quadratic to zero. Line 6 substitutes line 5 into the averaged quadratic. With equal curvatures \(\kappa_l = \kappa\), the right side of line 6 is \(\kappa \hat B_c / 2\). The empirical curve is a step function and has no curvature, so for it the formula is an approximation that the simulation compares with the observed gap. The paper uses the result in the Methods and the note on the order of pooling; the unit tests of the pooling rules check lines 1 to 3 on curves in code (a gap of exactly zero for identical curves), and the package’s known-answer tests on synthetic quadratic curves find line 6 to machine precision.

S1.4 The covariance split

Write the \(m\)-th imputed curve of resample \(b\) as \(\hat J_{bm} = A_b + e_{bm}\), with \(A_b\) the curve the resample would give with infinitely many imputations and \(e_{bm}\) the imputation noise, independent across \(m\) given the resample, with mean zero and covariance \(W\). Then \[ \begin{aligned} \bar J_b &= A_b + M^{-1} \textstyle\sum_m e_{bm}, \\ \mathrm{Cov}(\bar J_b) &= \mathrm{Cov}(A_b) + W / M = V, \\ \mathrm{E}\{(M-1)^{-1} \textstyle\sum_m (\hat J_{bm} - \bar J_b)(\hat J_{bm} - \bar J_b)^\top\} &= W, \\ \mathrm{Cov}(A_b) + W / L &= V - W / M + W / L . \end{aligned} \] Line 1 averages the \(M\) imputations. Line 2 uses the independence of the noise from \(A_b\) and across imputations. Line 3 is the unbiasedness of the sample covariance of \(M\) draws about their mean. Line 4 is the covariance of an estimate built from \(L\) imputations, written in terms of what the resamples estimate; with \(L > M\) it is smaller than \(V\). The bootstrap supplies \(\mathrm{Cov}(A_b)\) as the sampling covariance of the data’s own curve when the resample mimics the sample4. The paper uses the result for both bands and both sets; the known-answer test of the covariance split, on synthetic resamples with known parts, checks a diagonal and an off-diagonal entry.

S1.5 The comparison-based set holds the best threshold

Let \(k^*\) be the grid point with the largest \(J(c_k)\). If every comparison of \(k^*\) with another grid point is within its bound, \[ \begin{aligned} \{\bar J(c_j) - \bar J(c_{k^*})\} - \{J(c_j) - J(c_{k^*})\} &\le q_D\,\mathrm{SE}_{jk^*} \quad \text{for every } j \ne k^*, \\ J(c_j) - J(c_{k^*}) &\le 0, \\ \bar J(c_j) - \bar J(c_{k^*}) &\le q_D\,\mathrm{SE}_{jk^*}, \end{aligned} \] then \(k^* \in S_C\). Line 1 is the event. Line 2 holds because \(k^*\) is best. Line 3 adds lines 1 and 2, which is the condition for membership. The event of line 1 has probability 95% in the limit when the differences are jointly normal with covariance from \(\Sigma\) and \(q_D \ge q_{k^*}\); the largest per-point quantile \(q_D = \max_k q_k\) meets that whichever point is best. The plug-in value \(q_{\hat k}\) equals \(q_{k^*}\) when \(\hat k = k^*\) and otherwise carries no guarantee. The paper uses the result in the Methods; the known-answer tests check the critical value for two independent coordinates, \(\Phi^{-1}(0.95)\), and that a set built on the true curve holds the best grid point.

S1.6 One cutoff per stratum

A rule that calls a person positive when \(X > c(V)\), with one cutoff for each value \(v\) of a discrete covariate \(V\), has Youden index \[ \begin{aligned} J_{\mathrm{rule}} &= P\{X \le c(V) \mid D = 0\} - P\{X \le c(V) \mid D = 1\} \\ &= \textstyle\sum_v \{w_0(v) F_0(c(v) \mid v) - w_1(v) F_1(c(v) \mid v)\}, \end{aligned} \] with \(w_d(v) = P(V = v \mid D = d)\). Line 1 is the definition. Line 2 conditions on \(V\). Each term of the sum depends on one cutoff only, so the rule is maximized term by term, and the population-optimal cutoff of stratum \(v\) maximizes \(w_0(v) F_0(c \mid v) - w_1(v) F_1(c \mid v)\). With densities, its first-order condition is \(w_0(v) f_0(c \mid v) = w_1(v) f_1(c \mid v)\), while the stratum’s own Youden cutoff solves \(f_0(c \mid v) = f_1(c \mid v)\). The two agree when \(w_0(v) = w_1(v)\). At the stratum’s own cutoff the derivative of the population criterion is \(\{w_0(v) - w_1(v)\} f_0(c \mid v)\), so a stratum that holds a larger share of the controls than of the cases has a population-optimal cutoff above its own, for a curve with one peak. The paper uses the result in the application; the tests of StratumCutoffs() check that equal shares give the stratum’s own cutoff and that a larger share of controls does not lower it.
